deep_dive_html:
The Perils of Unilateral Relocation Rights

For franchisees, a relocation clause is not merely a logistical inconvenience; it is a potential existential threat to the business unit. Landlords frequently insert relocation provisions that grant them the unilateral right to move your operations to any available space within the development. The danger lies in the lack of specific, measurable criteria for what constitutes comparable space. Without rigorous definitions, a landlord can migrate a high-performing corner unit to a dead-end corridor, effectively stripping the location of its revenue-generating potential while technically adhering to the lease terms.

The exploitation of these clauses typically manifests in three critical areas:

  • Visibility and Frontage: Moving from a prominent street-facing position to an interior mall position significantly degrades brand exposure and customer acquisition.
  • Construction and Capital Expenditure: Landlords often attempt to shift the burden of make-good costs, including signage, flooring, and utility reconfiguration, onto the tenant.
  • Franchisor Compliance: A relocation may inadvertently violate your franchise agreement’s territory or radius restrictions, potentially triggering a default with your franchisor.

Establishing Rigorous Relocation Standards

To protect your investment, you must move beyond the vague comparable space language found in standard-form leases. An elite negotiation strategy focuses on establishing a Relocation Standard that is mathematically and operationally verifiable. You must demand that any replacement premises meet specific benchmarks regarding square footage, ceiling height, loading capabilities, and, most importantly, visibility and foot traffic metrics.

Furthermore, a robust relocation clause must include a comprehensive Cost Indemnification provision. This ensures the landlord is responsible for all direct and indirect costs associated with the move, including permit fees, architectural drawings, and the physical installation of brand-standard signage. Finally, negotiate a Right of Refusal or a Termination Right if the proposed new space fails to meet these pre-negotiated criteria. This prevents the landlord from forcing you into a sub-standard location that compromises your long-term profitability.
